subject: programming-and-data-structures

chosen.title: Recursion Notes for GATE Exam
chosen.note: the direct/indirect split and the tail, head, tree and nested shapes with their stated time and space costs
chosen.why: the only source read this run that names all five recursion shapes in one place with a stated time and space cost for each, which is the enumeration the taxonomy card and the linear/tree card are built on

chosen.title: Recursion (computer science)
chosen.note: base case and recursive case, the induction analogy, the call stack and the textbook examples
chosen.why: the cleanest statement of the base case and recursive case as a definition, with the induction analogy that turns 'is this recursion correct' into an induction argument, and the binary-search example that motivates the halving card

chosen.title: Tail call
chosen.note: tail position, frame reuse, and the reduction of stack space from O(n) to O(1)
chosen.why: the only source read that defines tail position precisely and states that frame reuse reduces O(n) stack to O(1) while remaining an implementation choice rather than a language guarantee, which is the whole content of the tail-call card

chosen.title: C Recursion
chosen.note: stack frames pushed and popped, the fixed stack region, stack overflow, and the recursion-versus-iteration costs
chosen.why: the only source read that describes the frame push and pop cycle, the fixed stack region and stack overflow as one mechanism, which the depth and space cards depend on

chosen.title: Basic Recursion MCQs: 12 Solved C Questions with Step-by-Step Explanations
chosen.note: descent against unwinding, a base case that is never reached, counting invocations, and static state across calls
chosen.why: the only source read that separates descent from unwinding as a rule and works it through GATE questions, including a base case that is never reached and static state followed across calls; three cards draw their trap fields from it

chosen.title: C mein Programming, tatha Punaraavartan - chapter notes (Devanagari)
chosen.note: the naive-Fibonacci call count 2F(n+1)-1, the 2^n-1 Hanoi moves, and the distinction between the number of calls and the stack depth
chosen.why: the only GATE-framed source that gives the 2F(n+1)-1 Fibonacci call count, the 2^n-1 Hanoi move count and the rule that stack depth is the height of the recursion tree and not the number of calls; it is also the only readable non-English source, and its four translated sentences are marked as translated on the cards that use them
